Lab Insights

Disclaimer: educational information only — not a diagnosis. This tool compares your numbers to general reference ranges; it does not prescribe medicine. Please review your results, and any medication or supplement decisions, with a doctor.

Upload a lab report (text-based PDF) or add values yourself — we'll flag anything outside the normal range, what it relates to, and food-based remedies.

Tracker

Pick a reading, add a value, and it gets its own section below. Colours show how your latest reading compares:

  • Green — the latest reading is within the acceptable range
  • Red, green side bar — the bar is half red, half green: outside the range, but closer to it than the previous reading (improved)
  • Red, orange side bar — the bar is half red, half orange: outside the range, and unchanged from the previous reading
  • Red — outside the range, and further from it than the previous reading, or no previous reading to compare with
  • Grey — no range to compare against

Weight is saved with your height, and judged against the healthy BMI range (18.5–24.9) for that height. Height shows green when it is higher than the previous reading. Blood Pressure judges systolic and diastolic together. Each reading in a list is coloured the same way against the one before it.

Educational only — ranges are general adult references, not a diagnosis. Readings stay on this device.

Water

Drink steadily through the day rather than trying to catch up all at once.

Take small, comfortable sips and swallow slowly. You do not need to gulp or force a full glass at once.
  • Slow sipping is more comfortable and may reduce bloating or stomach discomfort from drinking too quickly.
  • Pause between sips and stop when comfortably hydrated; avoid forcing excess water.
  • Drink more when it is hot or you are active, and follow any fluid limits advised by your clinician.

Walk

Short movement breaks to offset long sitting.

Stand, stretch or walk for 2–5 minutes at each reminder.
  • Improves circulation and reduces stiffness
  • Eases posture strain
  • Gives a small energy and focus boost

Eyes (20-20-20)

Give your eyes a break from screens.

The 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet (6 m) away for 20 seconds.
  • Reduces eye strain, dryness and blurred vision
  • Fewer screen-related headaches
  • Encourages blinking, which re-moistens the eyes

Eyes (Exercise)

A guided exercise for your eye muscles.

Follow the moving dot through seven patterns: zigzag, figure-8, loop, star, cross and row scan.
  • Up to 2 sessions a day: morning and evening
  • Each session lasts 2:15 — don't repeat it back-to-back
  • 3–5 days a week; rest on the other days

Checks

Wake-up time

3:00 – 4:30 AM is far earlier than the body's natural rhythm and usually cuts sleep short — red zone.
4:30 – 5:30 AM works for early risers used to it, but can still shorten sleep for most people — orange zone.
5:30 – 6:30 AM lines up well with most people's natural cortisol rhythm and gives a calm morning before the day's demands start — green zone, the sweet spot.
6:30 – 7:30 AM is still a perfectly healthy, common wake time — orange-green.
7:30 – 9:00 AM tends to compress the rest of the day's routine into a shorter window — orange zone.

☀️ Morning

  1. Rub your palms together briskly for 10–15 seconds, with firm but comfortable friction, until they feel warm.
  2. Close your eyes and cup your warm palms over them. Your palms (not your fingers) cover the eyes, your fingers rest on your forehead, and the heels of your hands sit on your cheekbones.
  3. Keep a small gap so nothing presses on the eyeballs.
  4. Hold for 30–60 seconds, breathing slowly.

The warmth and gentle cover relax the eye muscles and improve blood flow, easing your eyes into the day instead of going straight to bright light or a screen.

Rehydrates you after the overnight fast and kick-starts digestion. You lose water through breathing and sweat even while asleep.

How to drink it
  • Take small sips instead of big gulps, and finish the 1–2 glasses over about 5–10 minutes.
  • Pause between sips.
  • Warm (not hot) water is a good choice in the morning. It is gentle on an empty stomach, and many people find it helps the bowels move. Plain room-temperature water hydrates just as well, and water that is too hot can scald your mouth and throat.
Why slowly
  • Your body takes in water gradually, so more of it is used instead of passing straight through.
  • You swallow less air, so there is less bloating and burping.
  • An empty stomach copes better with small amounts. Gulping can leave you feeling heavy or queasy.

Your gut is most active in the morning, and a glass of water plus a little movement often brings on the urge.

How long to stay
  • Most people finish within 5 minutes. Try not to sit longer than about 10.
  • Go when you feel the urge, and leave your phone outside so you don't lose track of time.
If nothing comes
  • Don't strain or force it. Get up after a few minutes and try again later.
  • Walk around, drink another glass of water, or do a few minutes of gentle movement. The urge often follows a meal, especially breakfast.
  • Over the day, add fibre (fruit, vegetables, whole grains) and enough water, and keep a regular time so your body gets used to it.
  • Skipping a day now and then is normal. If it lasts several days, or comes with pain or blood, see a doctor.
What prolonged sitting or straining does
  • It raises pressure in the veins around the back passage, which can lead to piles (haemorrhoids) and small tears (fissures).
  • Over time, repeated straining can weaken the pelvic floor muscles.
  • Sitting for long, especially with a phone, can leave your legs numb and make you light-headed when you stand up.
Why it helps
  • Lifts mood and energy for the day and helps your heart, blood sugar and weight.
  • Morning daylight helps set your body clock, so you sleep better at night.
Watch out
  • Hard exercise on a completely empty stomach can make some people dizzy or weak.
  • Doing too much too soon strains joints and muscles.
  • Early-morning cold, heat or smog can make walking harder on the lungs.
Tips
  • Start easy, warm up for a few minutes, and sip water first.
  • Check the air quality, and pick a safe, well-lit route.
  • If you have a heart condition, or feel chest pain or unusual breathlessness, stop and talk to a doctor.
Best time
  • For your body clock and mood: soon after sunrise, within the first 1–2 hours of daylight. The light is bright while the heat and UV are still gentle. Sunrise changes with where you live and the season, so go by the sun rather than a fixed clock time.
  • This check is timed 75–105 minutes after your wake-up time. If you wake around sunrise, it lands in that window. If you wake later, sit a little shorter, or in light shade, once the sun feels strong.
  • For vitamin D, the sun has to be high: when your shadow is shorter than you are, or the UV index is 3 or more. That is usually late morning to early afternoon. About 10–15 minutes with your arms and legs uncovered is enough for most people. Longer mainly adds sunburn risk.
  • In winter at higher latitudes (for example much of Europe, Canada and the northern US) the sun may never get high enough to make vitamin D. Food or supplements matter more then, so ask your doctor.
  • Avoid long sits in the strongest midday sun, especially in hot places and in summer.
Why it helps
  • Morning light tells your brain it is daytime, so you feel alert now and sleepy at the right time at night.
  • It lifts mood and energy.
  • Your skin makes vitamin D in strong sun, and many people get too little. Early-morning sun makes only a little, so the higher-sun sit is the one that counts for vitamin D.
Watch out
  • Never look straight at the sun.
  • Window glass blocks the rays that make vitamin D, so sit outdoors, on a balcony, terrace or garden.
  • Fair skin burns faster. Stop if your skin turns red, or you feel dizzy.
  • If you take medicines or have a skin condition that makes you sun-sensitive, ask your doctor first.
Tips
  • Sit for 15–20 minutes, with your face and arms uncovered, and keep your phone aside. Make it shorter if the UV index is high.
  • Drink a glass of water afterwards if the sun was warm.
Why it helps
  • Refuels you after the overnight fast and steadies energy and focus.
  • Makes it easier not to overeat later in the day.
Watch out
  • A sugary or deep-fried breakfast spikes blood sugar, then leaves you tired and hungry.
  • Eating in a rush, or very late, upsets digestion.
  • Some people feel fine without breakfast, but a balanced one helps most people.
Tips
  • Combine protein (eggs, yogurt, beans or lentils, nuts) with fibre (oats, whole grains, fruit).
  • Skip sugary drinks, and sit down to eat.

🌤️ Afternoon

Why it helps
  • Gives fibre, vitamins and water, and keeps you full until lunch.
  • A healthy replacement for biscuits or a sugary snack.
Watch out
  • Juice has little fibre and raises blood sugar fast, so whole fruit is better.
  • Very sweet fruit in large amounts adds a lot of sugar, which matters if you have diabetes.
  • Sour fruit on an empty stomach can bother some people.
Tips
  • Eat one or two portions of whole, seasonal fruit.
  • Wash it well, and vary the kind from day to day.
Why it helps
  • Your main meal while digestion is strong, giving steady energy for the afternoon.
  • Eating at a regular time keeps hunger and cravings in check.
Watch out
  • A very heavy or oily lunch makes you drowsy in the afternoon.
  • Eating at your desk or on your phone leads to eating more without noticing.
  • Skipping lunch often leads to overeating at night.
Tips
  • Fill half your plate with vegetables or salad, add a protein such as lentils, beans, fish or eggs, and keep rice, bread or pasta moderate.
  • Chew slowly, and take a 5–10 minute walk afterwards.
Why it helps
  • Stops late-afternoon hunger so you don't overeat at dinner.
  • Keeps energy and focus steady until the evening.
Watch out
  • Chips, biscuits, sweets and fried snacks add salt, sugar and unhealthy fat.
  • Snacking out of habit or boredom adds extra calories.
  • A big snack too close to dinner spoils your appetite.
Tips
  • Choose a handful of nuts, fruit, yogurt, or roasted chickpeas.
  • Keep the portion small, and finish about two hours before dinner.

🌙 Evening & Night

Why it helps
  • Eating early gives your body time to digest before sleep, which helps sleep and weight.
  • A lighter evening meal is easier on your stomach.
Watch out
  • A late or heavy dinner can cause acidity and poor sleep, and adds weight over time.
  • Eating too little can leave you hungry and wake you up at night.
Tips
  • Keep it light and easy to digest, such as whole grains with vegetables and lentils, or soup.
  • Finish at least 2–3 hours before bed, and take a short walk afterwards.
Why it helps
  • Helps your mind wind down, so you fall asleep faster and sleep better.
  • Gives your eyes a rest after a day of screens.
Watch out
  • At first you may feel bored, or worry about missing a message.
  • The habit is hard to break, especially if the phone is also your alarm.
Tips
  • Charge the phone outside the bedroom, and use an alarm clock.
  • Set Do Not Disturb with a few allowed contacts for emergencies.
  • Replace scrolling with reading, light stretching or time with family.
Why it helps
  • 7–9 hours supports memory, mood, immunity, heart health and healthy weight.
  • A fixed bedtime sets your body clock, so you fall asleep more easily.
Watch out
  • Regularly sleeping under 6 hours is linked to poor focus, low mood, higher blood pressure and weight gain.
  • Irregular sleep times can leave you tired even after enough hours.
Tips
  • Keep the same bedtime every day, including weekends, in a cool, dark room.
  • Avoid caffeine in the afternoon and heavy meals or screens close to bed.
  • If you snore loudly, stop breathing in your sleep, or cannot sleep for weeks, see a doctor.

Mind

🌅

Rise & Reset

  • Morning mood is a teaser of the day. The decision is yours as to how the main picture should be.
  • Have a bath — wash off yesterday's dirt and let its thoughts rinse away.
  • Leave yesterday in yesterday — don't copy-paste it into today.
  • 0 expectations = ∞ happiness.
🚦

Traffic Therapy

  • Just think whether your reaction is worth it.
  • You are more valuable than your vehicle. So are others.
  • Be patient or become a patient.
💪

Work on Yourself

  • Learning something new for a few minutes a day brings returns with compound interest.
  • Mistakes aren't charity. Don't donate yours to others. Accept them.
  • Take criticism like a vaccine — brief sting, lasting immunity.
  • Jealousy makes you less. Put up a "No Entry" sign.
🌙

Sign-Off

  • The best medicine is sleep.
  • The side effect of thoughts in bed is sleeplessness.
  • Couldn't control your thoughts? Tonight's thought seeds are the next morning's harvest. So, choose what you sow.

Privacy Policy

Body & Activity section: The exercise and yoga recommendations are general fitness guidance based on the age group you select. No personal health information, biometric data, or activity history is collected, stored, or transmitted to any server — all calculations happen locally in your browser.

Food & Nutrition section: The dietary preference and age group you choose to generate nutrition suggestions are used only to compute recommendations within your current browser session. This information is not saved, logged, or shared with us or any third party.

Feedback: If you submit feedback, the name and message you provide are sent to us for review. Please avoid including sensitive personal or medical information in your feedback.

Advertising: This site displays advertisements, which may be served by third-party ad networks. These networks may use cookies, device identifiers, or similar technologies to show ads, measure their performance, and limit how often you see the same ad. This may include information about your general location, device type, and browsing activity on this site. We do not control how third-party ad networks use this data — please refer to their own privacy policies for details. You can manage or block ad-related data collection through your browser's cookie and privacy settings.

Backup & restore
Your vitals and settings are kept only on this device. Save them to a file now and then. If your browser's data is ever cleared, restore them from that file. An amber dot on the Backup icon means a backup is due: either none has been saved yet, or something changed since the last one.

Cookies

This site uses two kinds of local storage (cookies and similar browser storage):

Necessary Remembers things like your Body and Food choices, vitals entries, wake-up time, and reminder settings on this device. The app doesn't work properly without these, so they're always on.
Advertising Loads Google AdSense, which may set cookies to show and measure ads. If this is off, the ad script isn't loaded at all.

Notification Settings

The Alerts tab (Break / Walk / Drink reminders) can send you a browser notification when it's time — a popup in your taskbar on desktop, or a system notification on mobile. This needs your browser's permission first.
